the crossing answers reveal the kind: three national capitals, of Lebanon, Norway and South Korea

explanation.walkthrough: The four perimeter entries are filled from crossing letters; once two or three cities appear, the theme of capital cities makes the rest easy to complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Each is the seat of government of its nation, matching the preamble's unstated category of capital cities.

parts.note: there is no clue: the preamble says each side of the grid holds three proper nouns of one kind
the left-hand side holds the capitals of Azerbaijan, Bulgaria and Croatia

explanation.walkthrough: The left edge is built from the first letters of the across answers; the leading letter is shared with the top edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Each is the seat of government of its nation, matching the preamble's unstated category of capital cities.

parts.note: to be in is to be in favour, fashionable

indicators.note: redistributing something hands it out again in a new arrangement, so these letters are dealt out afresh

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A favoured nation has its foreign aid shared out again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' as an adjective means popular or in favour, as in 'the in crowd'.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a large nation of South Asia, so it is a straightforward example of a country.

clue.text: Good periods getting to secure higher areas

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast, so one piece wraps round and keeps hold of the other

parts.note: ups, as in ups and downs, are good times
to land something is to get it, as in landing a job

explanation.surface: Prosperous times allow people to buy up the hill country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' looks like a link word but supplies the inner piece; 'to secure' tells the outer piece to hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: Uplands are tracts of elevated ground, regions standing above the surrounding lowland country.

clue.text: Heads face up to old boy's poetry

parts.note: OB is the standard abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
verse is writing in metre, poetry

explanation.surface: Someone faces up to the poems written by a former pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' reads like a verb but belongs to a coin: the definition is the side of a coin bearing the head.
explanation.definitionFit: On a coin, the obverse is the principal side, usually showing a monarch's head, the one called heads when tossing.

indicators.note: a word meaning following in time places the second item behind the first in the line

parts.note: to lust after something is to crave it
rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane

explanation.surface: Someone has longed for a stiff drink after half a decade on the wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lust after' is a familiar phrase, but here 'after' only places the drink behind the craving.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustrum is a Latin-derived term for a period of half a decade, originally the interval between Roman censuses.

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: walking sticks and stakes are supports
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Hospital equipment such as braces and crutches includes gadgets that draw notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supports' reads as a verb, but it is a plural noun giving the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A shtick is a performer's signature gimmick or routine, a trick used to grab an audience's notice.

indicators.note: to review is to go over again and revise, so the letters are worked over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A legal instruction: look again at the riot prosecutions and impose a ban.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' sounds like a judicial process in this legal setting, but it only asks for the letters to be reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: To ostracise is to exclude someone from society or a group, shutting them out much as a ban does.

parts.note: there is no clue: the preamble says each side of the grid holds three proper nouns of one kind
the right-hand side holds the capitals of Peru, Belarus and Iran

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble warns that the first city here has two possible answers, since its middle letters are unchecked by any across entry; the official grid uses the Peruvian capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Each is the seat of government of its nation, matching the preamble's unstated category of capital cities.

clue.text: Soft digital covers Boy George adores

parts.note: a kid is a child, a boy
George was G in the old RAF phonetic alphabet
to adore is to love

explanation.surface: The singer Boy George is fond of soft gloves and nail decorations.
explanation.walkthrough: Boy George, the 1980s pop singer, must be split: one word gives a child, the other a letter. 'Digital' means relating to fingers, not computers.
explanation.definitionFit: Kid gloves are made of fine goatskin leather and so are soft coverings for the fingers, the body's digits.

clue.text: Emblem of a form of betting — the first of many

parts.note: the Tote is a pool betting system run at British racecourses

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only the initial is kept

parts.note: the initial of this word

explanation.surface: A symbol representing one style of gambling that comes first for most punters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tote is a pool betting system, where winners share the money staked, common at British racecourses.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an object or animal adopted as the symbol of a clan, an emblem of a group's identity.

clue.text: Comes across critic after opening of show

definitions.note: a verb phrase for a noun: a spanner is one that spans, comes across

indicators.note: following in sequence puts the second item behind the first
the opening of a word is where it starts, so only its initial is taken

parts.note: the initial of this word
a critic who pans a show, slating it, is a panner

explanation.surface: A reviewer arrives at the start of a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is stretched: something that spans a gap is a spanner, as a bridge comes across a river. The usual sense, a tool for nuts, is not the one meant.
explanation.definitionFit: To span is to stretch across, so a thing that spans, extending from one side to another, can loosely be called a spanner.

indicators.note: to play with something is to move it about freely, so the letters are toyed with into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Remembering a medieval miracle play, a drama about saints' lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miracle play' is a real phrase for a medieval religious drama, so 'play' hides its role as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall goods or a loan is to demand them back, which is to reclaim them, take them back into possession.

indicators.note: to show is to display or reveal, so the word on view lets part of itself be seen

parts.note: the three letters following the opening pair of this word

explanation.surface: The accounts reveal how little cash there is in the kitty.
explanation.walkthrough: The sou was an old French coin of tiny value, surviving in the phrase 'not a sou' for no money at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'not a sou' means penniless, so a single such coin stands for a trifling amount of cash.

parts.note: the fore is the front, as in the foreground
to see is to view

explanation.surface: Expecting a good view from the front row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front view' reads like a noun phrase, but the two words simply stack as a prefix and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To foresee events is to predict them before they happen, which is to expect or anticipate them.

clue.text: Trier somehow always one to get things back

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters end up in an order not yet given

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
ever means always, as in 'for ever'

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps trying is forever the one sent to fetch things.
explanation.walkthrough: Trier is also a German city, which tempts a solver toward geography in this grid of capitals.
explanation.definitionFit: A retriever is a gundog bred to fetch shot game, or anyone who recovers lost items and brings them back.

clue.text: Devious one up to be a general

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general in the American Civil War

explanation.surface: A scheming officer is in line for promotion to general rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to' looks like scheming ('up to something'), but 'up' alone signals the reversal and 'to be' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone slippery and evasive is called an eel, after the fish that is hard to hold, so a devious person fits.

parts.note: to miss something is to avoid it
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tries to dodge being put on a committee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One on' reads as a sequence instruction, but both words simply supply letters in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A mission is a group of envoys sent abroad to negotiate or represent a body, which is just what a delegation is.

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept and the rest dropped

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of this word

explanation.surface: A spare kitchen kept for routine use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' as a noun can mean coolness of manner, and that is the sense here.
explanation.definitionFit: Reserve means a cool, distant manner, and ice describes the same frosty aloofness in a person.

clue.text: Credential unfortunately leaving out end item

indicators.note: something that has gone badly has gone wrong, so the letters fall into a wrong order
leaving something out means omitting it, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written, before trimming and rearranging
taken as written; these three letters are the ones removed

explanation.surface: An unlucky omission of the final item in someone's qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End' looks like an instruction to drop the last letter, but it is the word itself that is taken out, its three letters scattered in the middle of the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: An article is a single thing among others, as in an article of clothing, so it equals an item.

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a cup is a drinking vessel
to list is to lean over, as a ship does

explanation.surface: A ship's crew cuts down the disorder on a list of things aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'List' and 'vessel' together suggest a ship tilting; the vessel is in fact a cup, though the list keeps its nautical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To clean up is to tidy, getting rid of dirt and clutter, which reduces disorder.

clue.text: Final recipient endures being out of order

indicators.note: something out of order is not in its proper sequence, so the letters must be reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: The last person to receive a faulty product puts up with it not working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' suggests a broken machine, fitting the consumer picture, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The end user is the person who ultimately uses a product, the last link in the supply chain, so its final recipient.

parts.note: a hen is a female bird; the 's links it to what follows
a peck is an old dry measure of capacity, a quarter of a bushel

explanation.surface: Someone knocks a bird for how much it can hold.
explanation.walkthrough: A peck is an old unit of dry volume, equal to two gallons, so 'capacity' stands for it; it also chimes with pecking birds.
explanation.definitionFit: To henpeck is to nag constantly, especially said of a wife domineering her husband with persistent fault-finding.

clue.text: They join up with egg producers who are after detailed promotional material

indicators.note: read as de-tailed, it means having the tail cut off, so the final letter goes
coming after something means following it, so this piece is placed behind the other

parts.note: hype is publicity material, with its last letter removed
hens are the birds that lay eggs

explanation.surface: People team up with poultry farmers who want thorough advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'thorough', but it is split as de-tailed: the tail of the publicity word is cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: A hyphen is the short dash linking two words or word parts, so hyphens are marks that connect things together.

clue.text: Cheek to marry in formal wear

parts.note: neck means cheek or nerve, as in having the brass neck
to tie the knot is to marry, so to tie is to join

explanation.surface: It takes nerve to get married dressed in black tie.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, neck means impudence, as in 'what a neck!' or 'brass neck'.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is a band of cloth knotted at the collar, a standard part of smart or formal attire.

indicators.note: to say a word is to speak it, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: Someone refuses an elderly army officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say no' reads as refusing, but 'Say' marks the sound of the old word for no.
explanation.definitionFit: Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals, executed in 1815, so he is a historical French military commander.

clue.text: A need is to provide liquid flavouring

indicators.note: something liquid flows and takes any shape, so the letters run into a new form

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A recipe calls for some liquid to add taste to a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liquid flavouring' looks like a single phrase, but 'liquid' belongs to the wordplay as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Aniseed is the liquorice-tasting seed of the anise plant, used to give drinks and sweets their taste.

parts.note: to pick is to choose
to axe something is to get rid of it

explanation.surface: Someone decides to do without an implement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To dispense with' reads as a link, but it is the second piece: to axe is to cut or scrap.
explanation.definitionFit: A pickaxe is a heavy digging implement with a pointed iron head, so it is a type of hand tool.

indicators.note: outing something means putting it out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written, before trimming
A is the abbreviation for away in football fixtures; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: Calling off the yearly trip somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annual outing' reads as a works trip; 'outing' is in fact the removal signal, and in sports results A stands for an away fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul a contract or marriage is to declare it void, so the verb is a formal way of cancelling.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old verb for eating greedily, also spelt ravin
second meaning: the large black crow

explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense survives chiefly in 'ravenous'; the bird sense is the familiar one.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to eat voraciously, the root of ravenous, while the noun names a large black member of the crow family.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an inducement or bribe, a come-on
second meaning: something added to a hot drink to change its taste

explanation.surface: A host invites a guest inside for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come on in' reads as a welcome, but it splits: a come-on is an enticement, and the rest describes a thing stirred into a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A sugar substitute is stirred into hot drinks, while a bribe or inducement offered to tempt someone is also called by this word.

the bottom edge holds the capitals of Switzerland, France and Germany

explanation.walkthrough: The bottom edge is built from the last letters of the down answers, sharing its corners with the two side edges.
